content: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will touch them. {{v:2}} In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died. Their departure was considered a disaster, {{v:3}} and their travel away from us ruin, but they are in peace. {{v:4}} For even if in the sight of men they are punished, their hope is full of immortality. {{v:5}} Having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; because God tested them, and found them worthy of himself. {{v:6}} He tested them like gold in the furnace, and he accepted them as a whole burnt offering. {{v:7}} In the time of their visitation they will shine. They will run back and forth like sparks among stubble. {{v:8}} They will judge nations and have dominion over peoples. The Lord will reign over them forever. {{v:9}} Those who trust him will understand truth. The faithful will live with him in love, because grace and mercy are with his chosen ones. {{v:10}} But the ungodly will be punished even as their reasoning deserves, those who neglected righteousness and revolted from the Lord; {{v:11}} for he who despises wisdom and discipline is miserable. Their hope is void and their toils unprofitable. Their works are useless. {{v:12}} Their wives are foolish and their children are wicked. {{v:13}} Their descendants are cursed. For the barren woman who is undefiled is happy, she who has not conceived in transgression. She will have fruit when God examines souls. {{v:14}} So is the eunuch which has done no lawless deed with his hands, nor imagined wicked things against the Lord; for a precious gift will be given to him for his faithfulness, and a delightful inheritance in the Lord’s sanctuary. {{v:15}} For good labors have fruit of great renown. The root of understanding can’t fail. {{v:16}} But children of adulterers will not come to maturity. The seed of an unlawful union will vanish away. {{v:17}} For if they live long, they will not be esteemed, and in the end, their old age will be without honor. {{v:18}} If they die young, they will have no hope, nor consolation in the day of judgment. {{v:19}} For the end of an unrighteous generation is always grievous.

facets.text: The passage overturns the appearance of death as defeat: the righteous who seem to perish in the eyes of the foolish are in fact secure "in the hand of God," untouched by torment and at peace. Their apparent disaster is a hidden triumph, and their hope is "full of immortality." This is one of the clearest Old Testament affirmations of a blessed life beyond death for the just.
facets.question: Why does the death of the righteous only look like a defeat?

facets.text: Suffering is reinterpreted as divine testing rather than divine abandonment. God tries the righteous "like gold in the furnace," and their light chastening prepares them to receive a great good, so that affliction becomes the proof and refinement of their worthiness for God. This transforms the problem of the suffering of the just into a pedagogy of purification.
facets.question: How can the suffering of good people be an act of God's refining love rather than punishment?

facets.text: The righteous are described as being accepted by God "as a whole burnt offering," giving their tested lives a sacrificial and liturgical meaning. Their martyrdom or affliction is not waste but an acceptable oblation, anticipating the Christian understanding that the self-offering of the faithful is united to sacrifice and pleasing to God.
facets.question: What does it mean that the lives of the righteous are received by God like a burnt offering?

facets.text: The reward of the just is not merely rest but active glory: in the time of their visitation they will shine, run like sparks among stubble, and judge nations and have dominion over peoples, while the Lord reigns over them forever. This eschatological vision grounds the New Testament promise that the saints will reign with Christ and share in his judgment.
facets.question: Will the righteous share in ruling and judging at the end of time?

facets.text: The destiny of the ungodly is presented as the intrinsic fruit of their own choices: because they neglected righteousness and revolted from the Lord, their hope is void, their toils unprofitable, and their works useless. Punishment here is not arbitrary but the self-inflicted emptiness of a life that despised wisdom and discipline.
facets.question: Is the punishment of the wicked something God imposes or something they bring on themselves?

facets.text: The passage boldly reverses conventional measures of blessedness by declaring the undefiled barren woman and the faithful eunuch truly fruitful. Though childless by worldly standards, their faithfulness earns them fruit when God examines souls and "a delightful inheritance in the Lord's sanctuary," teaching that spiritual fidelity, not physical progeny, is the real measure of a fruitful life.
facets.question: How can a childless but faithful person be more blessed than one with many descendants?

facets.text: In contrast to the fruitfulness of the faithful, the offspring of unlawful unions are said to vanish and bear no lasting honor, showing that mere biological continuation cannot secure a blessing without righteousness. The "root of understanding" cannot fail, but a lineage founded in transgression comes to a grievous end, whether it lives long or dies young.
facets.question: Why does the passage say the descendants of the wicked have no lasting future?

facets.text: The whole discourse hinges on knowing and trusting God: "those who trust him will understand truth," and the faithful "will live with him in love, because grace and mercy are with his chosen ones." The final destiny of the just is thus not merely reward but abiding communion with God, sustained by his grace and mercy rather than by human merit alone.
facets.question: What is the ultimate destiny of those who trust in God?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Wisdom 3 contrasts the hidden immortal destiny of the righteous—tested, refined, and glorified in God's hand—with the self-inflicted ruin of the ungodly, redefining true fruitfulness as faithfulness rather than worldly appearance or progeny.

[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The righteous who seem to die are actually secure in God's hand, at peace, and full of the hope of immortality; their apparent disaster is hidden triumph.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Suffering of the just is divine testing that refines them like gold, turning affliction into purification and preparation for great reward.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: God accepts the tested righteous \"as a whole burnt offering,\" giving their affliction a sacrificial, liturgical meaning fulfilled in Christian self-offering.
[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: The just will shine, judge nations, have dominion over peoples, and live under God's eternal reign, grounding the NT promise that saints reign and judge with Christ.
[MORAL | explicit]: The ungodly's punishment is the intrinsic emptiness of lives that despised wisdom and revolted from God—void hope and useless works.
[MORAL | traditional]: The undefiled barren woman and faithful eunuch are truly fruitful, since fidelity, not physical progeny, wins fruit and an inheritance in God's sanctuary.
[MORAL | explicit]: Offspring of unlawful unions vanish and gain no honor, showing biological continuation without righteousness secures no lasting blessing.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Those who trust God understand truth and live with him in love through grace and mercy, so the just attain abiding communion, not merely reward.
